new_statements.quote: Stress in Bobongko is predictably penultimate, with suffixation precipitating stress movement. Compare the two following word pairs: duangan [duˈaŋan] 'boat' duanganto [duaˈŋanto] 'our boat' konyuku [koˈɲuku] 'fingernail' konyukuung [koɲuˈkuːŋ] 'your fingernail'
new_statements.citation: Mead, David. 2001. A preliminary sketch of the Bobongko language. In Wyn D. Laidig (ed.), Studies in Sulawesi linguistics, part VII (NUSA 49), 61-94. Jakarta: Badan Penyelenggara Seri NUSA, Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya.
new_statements.locator: pp. 66-67, section 3.1 'Phonemes' (last paragraph of p. 66 and the example block at the top of p. 67); PDF pages 6-7 of the saved file
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; when a suffix or enclitic is added, stress shifts rightward so that it stays on the new penult (du'angan -> dua'nganto; ko'nyuku -> konyu'kuung). A final diphthong (-oy) counts as one syllable for the count.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only related remark (p. 67) is that penultimate stress on lumangoy 'swim' shows the final -oy to be a diphthong rather than two vowels, i.e. the rule is used to decide syllabification, not as an exception. The author (p. 61) calls the whole paper preliminary, based on one week of fieldwork in January 2001.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; the examples are isolated citation forms, stem versus stem+suffix/enclitic (possessive -to 'our', -ung 'your'). The rule is stated for the phonological word including suffixes, hence 'stress movement' under suffixation.
new_statements.identity_note: Mead 2001 describes the Bobongko of Lembanato village (Kilat Bay, Togian Island), the main community; the same language as Glottolog bobo1255 / ISO bgb. No dialect split is described; a splinter community at Tumbulawa (Batu Daka Island) is mentioned but not separately documented.

sources.citation: Sulawesi Language Alliance (David Mead), 'Bobongko' language page, sulang.org/languages/bobongko, last updated 2014-09-15.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; gives location, classification, vitality and a bibliography that lists only Adriani 1900, Mead 2001, Mead 2003, Noorduyn 1991 and Sneddon 1983 for the language (Wayback snapshot; sulang.org refuses connections 2026-09-17).

sources.citation: Mead, David. 2003. The Saluan-Banggai microgroup of eastern Sulawesi. In John Lynch (ed.), Issues in Austronesian historical phonology (Pacific Linguistics 550), 65-86. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU.
sources.note: Comparative-historical paper (sound correspondences, subgrouping); no statement on stress or accent in any language, only references to penultimate/antepenultimate syllable positions in sound changes (e.g. section 3.9 'Raising of PMP antepenultimate *a'). Open access via ANU Open Research, http://hdl.handle.net/1885/254172.
No phonology content; cites only Ethnologue, Glottolog and Mead 2003.
